ranksum¶

Wilcoxon rank-sum (Mann–Whitney) test for two independent samples.

Signature¶

RankSumResult ranksum(const pluss::Series& x, const pluss::Series& y, const TestOptions& options = {}, pluss::Config cfg = {});

What It Does¶

ranksum ranks the pooled observations (tied values share the average rank) and asks whether the values of x tend to be larger or smaller than those of y. The statistic rank_sum_x is the sum of the ranks of x; u_stat is the Mann–Whitney U, the rank sum minus its smallest possible value nx (nx + 1) / 2. Only the ordering of the data matters, so the test is robust to outliers and to skewness.

The p-value is exact for small samples (the smaller sample under 10 observations and fewer than 20 in all) and otherwise comes from the normal approximation with a continuity correction and a variance adjusted for ties; TestOptions::method forces either. stat is the corresponding z score.

Parameters¶

x

The first sample.

y

The second sample.

options (TestOptions)

alpha (default 0.05), tail (Tail::Both, Tail::Right or Tail::Left) and method (PValueMethod::Auto, Exact, Approximate; used only by the tests that have both forms).

cfg

the dtype and platform used for the computation; the default is evaluated in double precision on the CPU.

Returns¶

A RankSumResult. Its fields:

Field

Meaning

stat

the test statistic

pvalue

the probability, if the null hypothesis is true, of a statistic at least as extreme as the observed one

critical

the critical value of the statistic at level alpha

reject

true when pvalue < alpha

rank_sum_x

the sum of the ranks of x in the pooled sample

u_stat

the Mann–Whitney U statistic of x

effective_nx

finite observations used from x

effective_ny

finite observations used from y

Errors¶

  • No finite observation in either sample.

  • alpha outside (0, 1).

Practical Examples¶

Example 1¶

Do two machines produce different fill volumes?

#include <pluss/ma.h>

#include <iomanip>
#include <iostream>

namespace hyp = pluss::subsp::stats::inference::hypothesis;

int main() {
  std::cout << std::fixed << std::setprecision(4);
  const auto a = pluss::make_series(std::vector<double>{5.1, 4.9, 6.2, 5.8, 6.0, 5.5, 5.3, 6.1}, {8}, as_f64());
  const auto b = pluss::make_series(std::vector<double>{4.8, 5.2, 5.0, 4.7, 5.6, 4.9, 5.1, 4.6, 5.3}, {9}, as_f64());

  const auto r = hyp::ranksum(a, b);
  std::cout << "rank sum of A " << r.rank_sum_x << ", U " << r.u_stat << ", z " << r.stat << ", p " << r.pvalue << (r.reject ? " (reject)" : " (keep)") << "\n";
}

Output

rank sum of A 96.5000, U 60.5000, z 2.3137, p 0.0164 (reject)

The rank sum of A is 96.5 and the U statistic 60.5, giving z 2.31 and p 0.0164: the fill volumes of the two machines differ. The test uses only the ranks, so it does not depend on the shape of the distributions.

Example 2¶

Exact and approximate p-values for samples with ties.

#include <pluss/ma.h>

#include <iomanip>
#include <iostream>

namespace hyp = pluss::subsp::stats::inference::hypothesis;

int main() {
  std::cout << std::fixed << std::setprecision(4);
  const auto x = pluss::make_series(std::vector<double>{3, 5, 5, 7, 8, 8, 8, 10, 12, 12, 14, 15}, {12}, as_f64());
  const auto y = pluss::make_series(std::vector<double>{4, 5, 6, 8, 8, 9, 11, 11, 13, 13, 13, 16, 18, 20}, {14}, as_f64());
  hyp::TestOptions exact, approximate;
  exact.method = hyp::PValueMethod::Exact;
  approximate.method = hyp::PValueMethod::Approximate;
  std::cout << "default     p " << hyp::ranksum(x, y).pvalue << "\n";
  std::cout << "exact       p " << hyp::ranksum(x, y, exact).pvalue << "\n";
  std::cout << "approximate p " << hyp::ranksum(x, y, approximate).pvalue << "\n";
}

Output

default     p 0.2663
exact       p 0.2658
approximate p 0.2663

With ties the default p-value 0.2663 uses the normal approximation with a tie correction, and the exact p-value is 0.2658: the two agree to three decimals, and the decision is the same.

Example 3¶

One-sided alternative: does A tend to be larger than B?

#include <pluss/ma.h>

#include <iomanip>
#include <iostream>

namespace hyp = pluss::subsp::stats::inference::hypothesis;

int main() {
  std::cout << std::fixed << std::setprecision(4);
  const auto a = pluss::make_series(std::vector<double>{5.1, 4.9, 6.2, 5.8, 6.0, 5.5, 5.3, 6.1}, {8}, as_f64());
  const auto b = pluss::make_series(std::vector<double>{4.8, 5.2, 5.0, 4.7, 5.6, 4.9, 5.1, 4.6, 5.3}, {9}, as_f64());

  hyp::TestOptions options;
  options.tail = hyp::Tail::Right;
  const auto r = hyp::ranksum(a, b, options);
  std::cout << "p " << r.pvalue << ", critical z " << r.critical << "\n";
}

Output

p 0.0082, critical z 1.6449

One-sided, the p-value halves to 0.0082 and is compared with the critical z 1.645.
